action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG on arrival

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) before pacing is secured
Do not start or increase vasodilators (nitrates, dihydropyridines) in severe aortic stenosis with hypotension
Do not discharge before a permanent pacing system is implanted
Do not give cefazolin or another cephalosporin as device prophylaxis
required_recommendations: Recognise complete AV block with a wide escape, from calcific aortic valve disease extending into the conduction system, together with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, as the cause of the exertional syncope

Admit to a monitored bed with continuous ECG monitoring and transcutaneous pacing pads; temporary transvenous pacing if the escape becomes unstable or pause-dependent ventricular arrhythmia recurs before implantation

Implant a permanent pacing system during this admission (ESC 2021 Class I for third-degree AV block); with LVEF 40% and near-complete ventricular pacing expected, consider CRT or conduction-system pacing rather than right ventricular pacing (ESC 2021), timed with the valve plan

Refer to the Heart Team for aortic valve intervention for symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (ESC/EACTS 2025 Class I); at 74 with a trileaflet valve, TAVI is favoured if transfemoral access is feasible
Hold amlodipine and tamsulosin and review losartan (blood pressure 94/55 mmHg, severe aortic stenosis, potassium 5.3 mEq/L, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL)
Use non-cephalosporin antibiotic prophylaxis (for example vancomycin) at device implantation because of his cephalosporin allergy
Investigate the microcytic anaemia (iron studies, gastrointestinal source including angiodysplasia associated with aortic stenosis) before valve intervention

Advise no driving until the pacemaker is implanted and the severe aortic stenosis has been treated: Group 1 drivers may resume 1 week after pacemaker implantation for the arrhythmic cause, and only once the structural cause is successfully treated (ESC 2018)

avoided_actions.rationale: No fever, meningism or encephalopathy: CSF has no role; the syncope is explained by complete AV block from calcific aortic valve disease with severe aortic stenosis.

Exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (ESC/EACTS 2025); the cause is complete AV block from calcific aortic valve disease with severe aortic stenosis.
EEG is not recommended in syncope (ESC 2018 Class III); there were no seizure features and the cause is complete AV block from calcific aortic valve disease with severe aortic stenosis.
Brain MRI is not indicated in syncope without focal signs (ESC 2018 Class III); the cause is complete AV block from calcific aortic valve disease with severe aortic stenosis.

differential.diagnosis: Severe aortic stenosis with exertional syncope
differential.key_features: Echo confirms severe stenosis (AVA 0.9 cm2, mean gradient 42 mmHg) and the events were exertional, so fixed outflow obstruction contributes; telemetry documents complete AV block with a 26-40 bpm escape, and both need treatment.
LVH, LVEF 40% and QTc above 500 ms are a substrate, but telemetry shows only three 3-5 beat runs after long escape intervals and no sustained VT; the near-syncope coincided with a rate of 28 bpm.
Troponin I is only minimally raised (0.06 ng/mL), as expected with severe aortic stenosis, LVEF 40% and bradycardia; no chest pain, no ST elevation.
Sinus rhythm at about 80 bpm runs independently of the ventricles: the block is AV, not sinus.
Exertional collapse without prodrome in a 74-year-old with complete AV block and severe aortic stenosis is not vasovagal.

Tilt and exercise testing are contraindicated in severe aortic stenosis

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Severe calcific aortic stenosis is a well-recognized cause of complete heart block due to extension of calcification from the aortic annulus into the adjacent conduction system (His bundle, proximal bundle branches)
Exertional syncope in the setting of aortic stenosis is a red flag for severe disease and carries prognostic significance indicating the need for valve intervention
Complete heart block with a wide-complex escape rhythm indicates an infranodal block, which is less likely to respond to atropine and more likely to require pacing
Prolonged QTc (>500 ms) in the setting of severe bradycardia significantly increases the risk of torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death
Exercise stress testing is absolutely contraindicated in severe symptomatic aortic stenosis
metadata.difficulty_rationale: ECG-diagnostic complete AV block with three required actions (ECG, TTE, telemetry); the nuance is the coexisting severe aortic stenosis: valve intervention, the pacing mode at LVEF 40%, contraindicated tilt and exercise testing, and vasodilator withdrawal.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Simmons is a 74-year-old man with a history of moderate aortic stenosis, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed sudden collapse. According to his wife, the patient was walking up the stairs to the second floor of their home at approximately 6:45 PM when he suddenly dropped to the ground on the landing without any warning. She was walking behind him and saw his body go limp as he fell forward, landing on his right side. She reports that he appeared very pale and his lips looked bluish for several seconds. She did not observe any jerking, shaking, stiffening, or rhythmic limb movements during the event. He was unresponsive for approximately 15 to 20 seconds, and then his eyes opened and he began speaking immediately, asking his wife why she was screaming and what had happened. He had no confusion, disorientation, or drowsiness after the event, and he was able to describe exactly what he had been doing before he blacked out. There was no tongue biting, no urinary or fecal incontinence, and no witnessed seizure-like activity. The patient himself recalls feeling completely well one moment and then suddenly waking up on the floor the next, with no preceding lightheadedness, nausea, chest pain, palpitations, or visual changes. Over the past six to eight weeks, he reports three prior episodes of near-syncope where his vision would suddenly go gray and he would feel as if he were about to pass out, each lasting a few seconds. Two of these occurred while climbing stairs and one while pushing a shopping cart at the grocery store. He has also noticed progressive exertional fatigue and dyspnea on exertion that has worsened over the past two to three months, to the point where he can no longer walk more than a block without needing to rest. He has a known cardiac murmur that he was told was getting worse at his last cardiology visit six months ago, but he missed his follow-up appointment. He denies fever, recent illness, chest pain at rest, orthopnea, or lower extremity edema.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration or evidence of oral trauma. No urinary incontinence noted. No scalp wound, haematoma or facial injury. Right hip tenderness from fall but no deformity. No bruising pattern suggestive of prolonged convulsive activity.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing normal bilaterally without dysmetria or intention tremor. Heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. No relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopic exam shows mild arteriolar narrowing bilaterally consistent with chronic hypertension, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus or diplopia. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch and pinprick in all three divisions bilaterally. Jaw strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation, no facial droop. CN VIII: Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, uvula midline, gag reflex present. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue protrudes midline, no atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal stride length and arm swing. Slightly wide base. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech is fluent with normal rate, volume, and prosody. No dysarthria or aphasia. Attention intact, able to perform serial sevens correctly. Recalls 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No confusion or post-ictal features at time of examination.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal, no rigidity, spasticity, or cogwheeling. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups tested bilaterally including deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, finger abductors, hip flexors, quadriceps, hamstrings, ankle dorsiflexors, and plantarflexors. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout upper and lower extremities. Proprioception intact at bilateral great toes. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral great toes and medial malleoli, consistent with mild length-dependent peripheral neuropathy.
